title: Counted and Camped in Order
subtitle: Numbers 1 to 4, Berean Standard Bible
description: Israel is counted as an army and camped in order around the tent, and the Levites are set apart to carry what no one may touch.
paragraphs: One month after the tabernacle went up at the foot of Mount Sinai, God spoke to Moses from inside it again. The laws of Leviticus had filled the space between the mountain and the camp. Now the camp was going to move, and before a people can march, someone has to know how many of them there are.
"On the first day of the second month of the second year after the Israelites had come out of the land of Egypt, the LORD spoke to Moses in the Tent of Meeting in the Wilderness of Sinai. He said:"

The command was a census. Moses and Aaron were to number the whole congregation of Israel by their clans and families, listing every man by name, one by one: every male twenty years of age or older who could serve in Israel's army. One leader from each tribe was named to stand with them and help, the heads of the clans of Israel. The book gives all twelve names. Reuben's leader was Elizur son of Shedeur. Judah's was Nahshon son of Amminadab. Dan's was Ahiezer son of Ammishaddai, and so on through the tribes, twelve men the reader will meet again at the head of the march and at the altar with their offerings.

This count was not a count of everyone. It was a count of an army. The land God had promised had people living in it, and Israel was not being led there as a crowd of refugees. It was being organized as a force that could take it.

The counters went tribe by tribe, clan by clan, name by name, and the totals came back uneven, the way real families are uneven. Judah was the largest, 74,600 men. Manasseh was the smallest, 32,200. Dan stood second at 62,700, and little Benjamin counted 35,400. Every tribe's number ends the same way in the text, given to the last fifty men, because every man had been named.
"And all those counted totaled 603,550."
One tribe is missing from that number, and the text stops to explain why. The Levites were not numbered with the others.

"Do not number the tribe of Levi in the census with the other Israelites. Instead, you are to appoint the Levites over the tabernacle of the Testimony, all its furnishings, and everything in it. They shall carry the tabernacle and all its articles, care for it, and camp around it."

When the camp moved, the Levites took the tent down. When the camp stopped, they put it up. No one else was to come near the tabernacle when it was being moved, on pain of death. And their camping place was the ring closest to the tent on every side.
"But the Levites are to camp around the tabernacle of the Testimony and watch over it, so that no wrath will fall on the congregation of Israel."

The Levites were a buffer of men standing between a holy tent and a careless nation. Leviticus had shown what happened when men came near God's fire the wrong way, in the deaths of Aaron's two oldest sons. That lesson is built into the geography now. The whole congregation would camp around the Levites. Only the Levites would camp around God.
Chapter 2 lays the whole camp out like a map, and it is the same square a reader has seen before, walked around one piece at a time in Exodus. Now it is filled with people.

On the east side, toward the sunrise, under one standard: Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun, 186,400 men in all. They were to set out first. On the south side, under the standard of Reuben: Reuben, Simeon, and Gad, 151,450. They were to set out second. In the middle of the camps, the Tent of Meeting was to travel with the camp of the Levites, each tribe setting out in the order it had encamped, every man in his place under his standard. On the west side, under the standard of Ephraim: Ephraim, Manasseh, and Benjamin, 108,100. They were to set out third. On the north side, under the standard of Dan: Dan, Asher, and Naphtali, 157,600. They were to set out last, under their standards.

The chapter ends by counting the census a second time, from the other direction: the total of those counted in the camps, by their divisions, was 603,550. The number that came out of the name-by-name count and the number that fills the four sides of the square are the same number. Then the sentence this book will say again and again in its good moments: the Israelites did everything the LORD commanded Moses. They camped under their standards in this way, and they set out in the same way, each man with his clan and his family.

Chapter 3 counts the one tribe the first count left out, and counts it differently. The Levites were numbered from a month old, every male, because their service was not war. It was inheritance by birth into the work of the tent.

Aaron's family comes first, and the record is honest about it. Aaron's sons were Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. Nadab and Abihu died in the presence of the LORD when they offered unauthorized fire in the Wilderness of Sinai, and since they had no sons, Eleazar and Ithamar served as priests in their father's lifetime. The census chapter does not skip over the family's dead. It counts the living with their names standing in the record next to them.

Then the three Levitical families, and each one gets a side of the tent and a job. The Gershonites, 7,500 males, camped on the west, behind the tabernacle, and their charge was the tent itself: its curtains, the tent and its covering, the curtain for the entrance, the hangings of the courtyard and its entrance, and the cords. The Kohathites, 8,600, camped on the south side, and theirs were the duties of the sanctuary: the ark, the table, the lampstand, the altars, the articles of the sanctuary used in ministering, and the curtain. The Merarites, 6,200, camped on the north side, and theirs was the frame: the boards of the tabernacle, its bars, pillars, bases, and all its equipment. Over all the Levites stood Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, chief of their leaders, with oversight of those responsible for the duties of the sanctuary.
"The total number of Levites that Moses and Aaron counted by their clans at the LORD's command, including all the males a month old or more, was 22,000."

Then the count turns into an exchange, and the exchange reaches back to the night Israel left Egypt. On the day God struck down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, He consecrated every firstborn in Israel to Himself, man and beast. The firstborn belonged to Him. Now He was taking substitutes.
"Behold, I have taken the Levites from among the children of Israel in place of every firstborn Israelite from the womb. The Levites belong to Me,"

So Moses counted the firstborn too, every male of the Israelites a month old or more, by name: 22,273. The Levites numbered 22,000. The firstborn outnumbered their substitutes by 273 men, and a substitute system in this book does not round off. Each of the 273 was to be redeemed at five shekels a head, by the sanctuary shekel.
"To redeem the 273 firstborn Israelites who outnumber the Levites, you are to collect five shekels for each one, according to the sanctuary shekel of twenty gerahs."

Five times 273 is 1,365 shekels, and that is the figure the chapter gives for the money Moses collected from the firstborn of Israel. He gave the redemption money to Aaron and his sons, in obedience to the word of the LORD. Two hundred seventy-three men walked through the camp that year carrying a price tag of five shekels each, the difference between what God had claimed on the night of the Exodus and the men He had accepted in their place.

Chapter 4 counts the Levites a third time, and this time the filter is working age. The men from thirty to fifty years old, everyone qualified to serve in the work at the Tent of Meeting, were numbered family by family for the carrying.

The Kohathites had the most holy things, and their work was the most dangerous work in the camp. When the camp was ready to move, Aaron and his sons went in first, alone, and covered everything. They took down the veil and covered the ark of the Testimony with it, then layers over that, a covering of fine leather and a cloth of blue, and set its poles in place. They wrapped the table, the lampstand, the altars, and every article in their own coverings and cloths, blue, purple, and scarlet. Only when Aaron and his sons had finished covering the holy objects and all their equipment could the Kohathites come in and lift them.
"But they must not touch the holy objects, or they will die."

Aaron and his sons assigned each Kohathite his task and what he was to carry, man by man, so that they would live and not die when they came near the most holy things. And even so, one more warning stands at the end of their instructions.
"But the Kohathites are not to go in and look at the holy objects, even for a moment, or they will die."
The holiest work in Israel was carrying furniture you were forbidden to see.

The Gershonites, 2,630 men of working age, carried the curtains, coverings, hangings, and cords, under the direction of Ithamar, Aaron's younger son. The Merarites, 3,200, carried the boards, bars, pillars, and bases, also under Ithamar. The Kohathites numbered 2,750. Eleazar, who stood over the Levites as a whole, had his own charge written down beside theirs: the oil for the light, the fragrant incense, the daily grain offering, and the anointing oil, and oversight of the entire tabernacle and everything in it.
"And the number of men was 8,580." Eight thousand five hundred eighty men, each one numbered by name and assigned his work and his burden, as the LORD had commanded Moses.

So the first four chapters of Numbers end with everything in its place, and nothing yet in motion. An army of 603,550 stands counted around a tent, in four camps under four standards, in an order it will both march in and sleep in. The tent at the center can be taken down, carried, and raised again by 8,580 named men who know exactly which pole, board, curtain, and vessel is theirs, down to the 273 men who were bought back at five shekels a head to balance the books of the firstborn.
It is the most organized Israel has ever been. What the camp does not have yet is a blessing spoken over it, rules for pushing uncleanness outside its borders before the march, or any orders to move.
And it has not yet been tested by a single mile of road.

title: Blessing, Trumpets, and the First March
subtitle: Numbers 5 to 10, Berean Standard Bible
description: The camp is blessed, given trumpets and a cloud to follow, and takes its first steps on the road.
paragraphs: The camp was counted and placed. Before it could move, it had to be cleaned, blessed, and given its marching orders, and that is what these six chapters do. Some of it is law the reader will recognize from Leviticus, wearing traveling clothes.

First, the borders of the camp were drawn the way Leviticus had drawn them around the tent. God told Moses to send away from the camp anyone with a skin disease, anyone with a bodily discharge, and anyone defiled by a dead body, male and female alike, so that they would not defile the camp where God dwelled in their midst. They were sent outside, the same outside the cleansed man of Leviticus waited in, hoping to be examined and brought back.

Then came a law that reaches back into Episode 1 of the last book and picks up its thread. When a man or woman committed any sin against another person, acting unfaithfully against the LORD, that person was guilty.
"And must confess the sin he has committed. He must make full restitution, add a fifth to its value, and give all this to the one he has wronged."

The fifth again: confession, repayment with more added, and if the wronged person had died with no close relative to receive it, the restitution went to the priest, along with the ram of atonement. Sin against a neighbor in this camp had paperwork, and the paperwork ended at the altar.

Chapter 5 also holds one of the strangest proceedings in the Bible, and the book tells it without explaining it, so it will be told here the same way. When a husband suspected his wife of unfaithfulness and no witness existed, he brought her to the priest with an offering of barley flour, no oil and no frankincense on it, because it was a grain offering for jealousy. The priest had the woman stand before the LORD with her hair unbound, and he made a water no kitchen in the camp would recognize: holy water in a clay jar with dust taken from the floor of the tabernacle stirred into it. He wrote the curses of the law in a book and washed the ink off into the water. The woman swore an oath accepting the outcome, and drank. If she had defiled herself, the water that brings a curse would enter her and cause bitter suffering, her belly would swell and her thigh would shrivel, and she would become a curse among her people. If she had not, she would be cleared and able to bear children. The husband was free from guilt in bringing the charge. The woman, if guilty, bore her iniquity. The text gives the rite and moves on. It does not say how often it was used, and no story in the Bible shows it happening.

Chapter 6 opens the door to a vow any Israelite could take, man or woman, rich or poor: the vow of a Nazirite, to separate himself to the LORD for a set time. For the whole period of the vow, no product of the grapevine, not wine, not vinegar, not grapes, not raisins, not even the seeds or the skins. No razor was to touch his head; he was to let the hair of his head grow long, because the symbol of his consecration to God was on his head. He could not go near a dead body, not even if his father or his mother or his brother or his sister died, a rule that put the Nazirite, for the length of his vow, under a version of the high priest's own restriction. If someone died suddenly beside him, his consecrated head was defiled, and the count started over after shaving and offerings on the seventh and eighth days. When the days were completed, he came to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting with a lamb, a ewe lamb, and a ram, with bread and drink offerings. His long hair was shaved at the entrance and put in the fire under the peace offering, and then he could drink wine again: the vow was over, and the hair that had marked it was ash on the altar.
Then the chapter changes key entirely. God gave Aaron and his sons the words they were to speak over Israel, and the words are not a law.
"Tell Aaron and his sons: This is how you are to bless the Israelites. Say to them:"
"May the LORD bless you and keep you; may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace."
"So they shall put My name on the Israelites, and I will bless them."

That blessing will be spoken over Israel's descendants for thousands of years, in rooms Aaron could not have pictured. In this camp it had a job: before the people moved a single mile, the priests stamped God's name on them with words about His face shining on them, and God took the actual blessing on Himself. The priests said it. He did it.

Chapter 7 is the longest chapter in the book, and it is one day told twelve times. On the day Moses finished setting up the tabernacle and anointed it, the leaders of Israel, the same twelve men who had assisted at the census, brought their dedication offerings. First came six covered wagons and twelve oxen, two leaders to a wagon, one ox each. Moses gave the wagons to the Levites who needed wheels: two wagons and four oxen to the Gershonites for the curtains, four wagons and eight oxen to the Merarites for the heavy frames and boards. The Kohathites got none, because their service was the holy things, and those were carried on shoulders.

Then, one leader on each of twelve days, came the identical gift, and the text records it in full twelve times over. A silver plate of 130 shekels and a silver bowl of 70 shekels, both filled with fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering. A gold pan of 10 shekels, full of incense. A young bull, a ram, and a male lamb a year old for a burnt offering. A male goat for a sin offering. And for the peace offering, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs a year old. Nahshon of Judah brought his on the first day. Nethanel of Issachar on the second. Elizur of Reuben, who had led the census count, on the fourth. So it went, tribe by tribe, page by page, until Gamaliel and Abidan and Ahira had brought theirs and the dedication of the altar was complete, with the chapter's totals at the end: twelve of everything, counted like the people were counted. When Moses went into the Tent of Meeting to speak with the LORD, he heard the voice speaking to him from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim. The long list had been leading somewhere after all. The tent worked. God talked in it.

Chapter 8 set the Levites apart for their service in a ceremony the whole congregation watched. The Levites were sprinkled with the water of purification. They shaved their whole bodies and washed their clothes. Two bulls were brought, and the Israelites laid their hands on the Levites, the way a man laid his hand on his offering, because the Levites were being given as an offering themselves: Aaron offered them as a wave offering from the Israelites before the LORD.

"And I have given the Levites as a gift to Aaron and his sons from among the Israelites, to perform the service for the Israelites at the Tent of Meeting and to make atonement on their behalf, so that no plague will come against the Israelites when they approach the sanctuary."

Their working years were set: from twenty-five years old a Levite could come to serve at the tent, and at fifty he retired from the work itself, though he could still assist his brothers and keep watch. The men who would carry God's house through the wilderness had a start date and a stop date, like the offerings had measures and the camp had sides.

A year out of Egypt, the second Passover came, and the camp kept it on the fourteenth day of the first month, at twilight, exactly as commanded. But a group of men came to Moses with a problem the law had not yet answered out loud. They were unclean because of a dead body, and they wanted to know why they should be kept from presenting the LORD's offering at its appointed time with everyone else. Moses did not improvise. He told them to wait while he listened for what the LORD would say. The answer widened the feast: a man unclean by a corpse, or away on a journey, could keep the Passover a month later, on the fourteenth day of the second month, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, nothing left till morning, no bone broken. A foreigner living among them who wanted to keep the Passover kept it by the same statute. One statute for the foreigner and the native of the land. The camp's God kept finding the man standing outside a rule and writing the door into the rule itself.

Above the whole arrangement sat the cloud. On the day the tabernacle was set up, the cloud had covered it, and from evening until morning it appeared like fire above the tent. Whether it stayed two days, a month, or a year, the Israelites camped as long as the cloud rested over the tabernacle, and when it lifted, they set out. Sometimes it rested only from evening till morning, and they set out in the morning. Sometimes it stayed, and they stayed, and kept the LORD's charge, and did not set out.
"They camped at the LORD's command, and they set out at the LORD's command; they carried out the LORD's charge according to His command through Moses."

Two trumpets of hammered silver were made for the last piece of machinery the march needed: a signal everyone could hear. Long blasts called the congregation together, or called only the leaders, or set the camps moving, east side first at one alarm, south side at the second. Short blasts in battle meant something no other signal in the camp meant: sound the trumpets when the enemy attacks, and you will be remembered before the LORD your God and saved. The trumpets were also blown over the sacrifices at the feasts and the new moons, a memorial before God. A camp this size could not be led by shouting. It would move, assemble, fight, and feast to the sound of silver.

On the twentieth day of the second month of the second year, the cloud lifted from above the tabernacle of the Testimony, and Israel set out from the Wilderness of Sinai in the order of their divisions, camp by camp, standard by standard, exactly the way chapter 2 had laid them out, the tent traveling in the middle with the Levites. They were bound for the wilderness of Paran.

Before the column moved, Moses made one personal request. Hobab, the son of his father-in-law Reuel the Midianite, was with the camp, and Moses asked him to come along. We are setting out for the place of which the LORD said, I will give it to you. Come with us, and we will treat you well, for the LORD has promised good things to Israel. Hobab said he would go back to his own land and his own people. Moses pressed him: please do not leave us, you know where we should camp in the wilderness, and you can be our eyes.
"If you come with us, we will share with you whatever good things the LORD gives us."

The text does not record Hobab's final answer, then or later. It records the march. Israel set out on a three-day journey from the mountain of the LORD, and the ark of the covenant went before them those three days, traveling ahead of the whole nation, to seek a resting place for them.
And Moses had a cry for the ark, at the start of every stage and at the end of it, two short sentences that turned a marching order into a battle and a homecoming.
Whenever the ark set out, Moses would say: "Rise up, O LORD! May Your enemies be scattered; may those who hate You flee before You."
And when it came to rest, he would say: "Return, O LORD, to the countless thousands of Israel."

The mountain of God was behind them. The camp that could not be blessed enough, counted enough, or organized enough was finally walking. It had taken two books of the Bible, a census, a law code, a priesthood, and a year at one mountain to get Israel moving toward the land it was promised in Genesis.
The road lasted three days before the complaining started.

title: Complaints, Quail, and Miriam
subtitle: Numbers 11 and 12, Berean Standard Bible
description: Three days in, the complaints begin: craving at Kibroth-hattaavah, then Miriam and Aaron turn on Moses.
paragraphs: Three days into the march, the complaints started, and they started at the edges.

The people began to complain about their hardship in the hearing of the LORD. When He heard them, His anger was kindled, and fire from the LORD blazed among them and consumed some of the outskirts of the camp. The people cried out to Moses. Moses prayed to the LORD, and the fire died down. The place was named Taberah, because the fire of the LORD had burned among them.

It was the first round of a cycle this book will run again and again: a complaint, a judgment, Moses praying for the very people who provoked it, and mercy. Taberah was only the warm-up. What came next had a menu attached.

The rabble among the people had a strong craving for other food, and the craving spread until the Israelites themselves were weeping, family after family at the entrances to their tents. Their complaint is quoted, and it is worth hearing in their own words, because it is a complaint about Egypt made by people standing three days out from the mountain of God.

"Who will feed us meat? We remember the fish we ate freely in Egypt, along with the cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic. But now our appetite is gone; there is nothing to see but this manna!"

Fish, freely, in Egypt. The slavery that Genesis and Exodus spent two books escaping had been recut in memory as a market with good produce. The manna they despised is described right after, almost in their defense and almost not: it was like coriander seed, the color of a pale resin. The people went out and gathered it, ground it in a hand mill or crushed it in a mortar, boiled it in a pot and made it into cakes, and it tasted like pastry made with oil. When the dew settled on the camp at night, the manna came down with it. It had fed them every day since the wilderness of Sin, without a field, a seed, or a market anywhere in reach. And a whole camp was standing at their tent doors crying over it, because it was not meat, and it was not Egypt.
The anger of the LORD was kindled greatly. And this time Moses broke too.

The burden speech Moses makes in chapter 11 is the most unguarded thing he says in the Bible so far, and it is aimed at God. Why have You brought this trouble on Your servant? Why have I not found favor in Your sight, that You have laid the burden of all these people on me?
"Did I conceive all these people? Did I give them birth, so that You should tell me, 'Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse carries an infant,' to the land that You swore to give their fathers?"
Where can I get meat for all these people, when they keep crying to me, give us meat to eat? I cannot carry all these people by myself. It is too burdensome for me.
"If this is how You are going to treat me, please kill me right now"
If he had found favor in God's eyes, he said, let God do that rather than let him see his own wretchedness.
The man who had argued God down from destroying Israel at the golden calf now asked to die rather than lead them another mile. God's answer was not rebuke. It was help, and meat, in that order.

Seventy elders of Israel, men Moses knew as leaders and officers of the people, were to be brought to the Tent of Meeting. God would come down and speak there, and take some of the Spirit that was on Moses and put that Spirit on them, and they would help him bear the burden of the people, so he did not have to bear it by himself. God's solution to Moses carrying too much was not a lighter people. It was more shoulders, with Moses' own Spirit spread across them.

And the people were to consecrate themselves for tomorrow, because they would eat meat, not for a day or two or five or ten or twenty days, but for a whole month, until it came out of their nostrils and they loathed it, because they had rejected the LORD who was among them and had wept before Him asking why they ever left Egypt. Moses, standing in front of that promise, did the arithmetic out loud. Here I am among 600,000 men on foot, and You say they will eat meat for a month? If all the flocks and herds were slaughtered, would it be enough? If all the fish of the sea were caught, would it be enough?
The LORD answered Moses: "Is the LORD's arm too short? Now you will see whether or not My word will come to pass."

Moses went out and spoke the LORD's words to the people, and he gathered the seventy elders and had them stand around the tent. The LORD came down in the cloud and spoke with him there, and He took some of the Spirit that was on Moses and placed that Spirit on the seventy elders. As the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied, though they never did so again. Two men on the list, Eldad and Medad, had remained in the camp instead of going out to the tent, and the Spirit rested on them there, and they prophesied in the camp. A young man ran and told Moses. Joshua son of Nun, Moses' attendant since his youth, spoke up.
"Moses, my lord, stop them!"
But Moses replied: "Are you jealous on my account? I wish that all the LORD's people were prophets and that the LORD would place His Spirit on them!"

It is the first time Joshua speaks in this book, and he speaks to defend Moses' honor against Moses' own wishes. The man who will one day lead the whole nation starts here, protective of a leader who does not want protecting. Moses, who had just asked God to kill him, answered his young attendant with the most generous sentence in the chapter.

Then the wind came. A wind sent by the LORD drove in quail from the sea and brought them down around the camp, about two cubits above the ground, for a day's journey in every direction. All that day, and all that night, and all the next day, the people stayed up gathering them. No one gathered less than ten homers. They spread them out all around the camp, meat as far as the eye could see, Egypt delivered in feathers.
"But while the meat was still between their teeth, before it was chewed, the anger of the LORD burned against the people, and the LORD struck them with a severe plague."
The place was called Kibroth-hattaavah, because there they buried the people who had craved other food. The meat had been promised for a month. The graves were dug on the first day of it.

Notice what God had and had not done in the whole affair. He had not refused the meat. He had promised it for a month, until it came out of their nostrils and they loathed it, and the quail came on the wind exactly as He said, farther than a man could walk in a day, in every direction. The craving was answered in full, and the answering was the judgment. He had not taken the burden off Moses either, by removing the people or by removing Moses, though Moses had asked for the second one outright. He had spread Moses' own Spirit across seventy men and told Moses his arm was not too short. Both halves of the camp, the leader who wanted to die and the people who wanted Egypt's food, got what they asked for, and both halves buried something at Kibroth-hattaavah.
From Kibroth-hattaavah the people traveled to Hazeroth, and there the complaint moved inside Moses' own family.
Miriam and Aaron criticized Moses because of the Cushite woman he had married. But the charge they spoke out loud was not really about the marriage, and the text quotes it plainly.
"Does the LORD speak only through Moses?" they said. "Does He not also speak through us?" And the LORD heard this.

Miriam was the prophetess who had led the women with tambourines at the sea. Aaron was the high priest whose robes had been sprinkled with blood and oil in front of the whole nation. Both of them had truly spoken for God, which is what made the claim dangerous. It was not false. It was aimed. And between their charge and God's answer, the narrator sets one sentence down about the man they were attacking, and it is the sentence this chapter is remembered by.
"Now Moses was a very humble man, more so than any man on the face of the earth."

Suddenly the LORD said to Moses, Aaron, and Miriam: come out, the three of you, to the Tent of Meeting. They came out. The LORD descended in a pillar of cloud and stood at the entrance to the tent and called Aaron and Miriam forward, and He drew the line they had blurred, in words that explain every dream and vision in the Bible around them.

"Hear now My words: If there is a prophet among you, I, the LORD, will reveal Myself to him in a vision; I will speak to him in a dream. But this is not so with My servant Moses; he is faithful in all My house."
"I speak with him face to face, clearly and not in riddles; he sees the form of the LORD. Why then were you unafraid to speak against My servant Moses?"

The anger of the LORD burned against them, and He departed. As the cloud lifted from above the tent, Miriam stood there covered in a skin disease, white as snow. Aaron turned toward her and saw it, and the high priest who a moment before had claimed a prophet's standing now pleaded like a brother. Do not hold this sin against us, he begged Moses, the sin we have committed in our foolishness. Do not let her be like a stillborn infant, its flesh half eaten away when it comes out of its mother's womb.
So Moses cried out to the LORD: "O God, please heal her!"

Five words in the English, and no hesitation in them. The man attacked an hour before prayed for his attacker on the spot, the way he had prayed at Taberah for strangers. God's answer was mercy with a sentence inside it. If her father had spit in her face, would she not be in disgrace for seven days? Let her be confined outside the camp for seven days. After that she may be brought back in.

So Miriam was shut outside the camp for seven days, in the place where the unclean waited, under the laws her own brother had received. And the people did not move on until she was brought in again. Six hundred thousand men, an army under four standards with an ark waiting to travel, sat in their tents for a week because the march would not leave Miriam behind.
After that, the people set out from Hazeroth and camped in the wilderness of Paran, at the edge of the land they had left Egypt to enter. The spies were about to go in.

title: The Spies and the Sentence
subtitle: Numbers 13 to 15, Berean Standard Bible
description: Twelve spies see the same land and bring back two reports, and a generation is sentenced to the wilderness.
paragraphs: From Paran, the wilderness camp could nearly see the end of the story. The land God had promised Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob lay just north of them. Before the army moved, God told Moses to send men in to look at it.
"Send out for yourself men to spy out the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the Israelites. From each of their fathers' tribes send one man who is a leader among them."

Twelve leaders, one from each tribe. The text names all twelve, and two of the names matter for the rest of the Bible. From the tribe of Judah, Caleb son of Jephunneh. From the tribe of Ephraim, Hoshea son of Nun, and the chapter pauses on him for one detail: Moses gave Hoshea the name Joshua. The attendant who had spoken out at Eldad and Medad has a new name now, given before the mission, and the mission would make it famous.

Moses' instructions were a surveyor's questions and a soldier's. See what the land is like, and whether the people living there are strong or weak, few or many. Whether the land is good or bad, whether the cities are camps or fortresses, whether the soil is fertile or unproductive, whether there are trees. And then, almost as an afterthought that turned out to be the point: be courageous and bring back some of the fruit of the land. It was the season for the first ripe grapes.

They went up through the Negev and into the hill country, as far north as Rehob toward Lebo Hamath, and down to Hebron, where the descendants of Anak lived, Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai. Hebron, the text notes in passing, had been built seven years before Zoan in Egypt. They came to the valley of Eshcol, and there they cut down a branch with a single cluster of grapes so large that they carried it on a pole between two of them. They took pomegranates and figs as well. The valley got its name from that cluster: Eshcol means cluster.
At the end of forty days, the twelve came back to Moses, Aaron, and the whole congregation in the wilderness of Paran at Kadesh, carrying the fruit and a report that begins like a promise kept.
"We went into the land to which you sent us, and indeed, it is flowing with milk and honey. Here is some of its fruit!"
Every word of that was true, and it was all the encouragement the report contained.
"Nevertheless, the people living in the land are strong, and the cities are large and fortified. We even saw the descendants of Anak there."

They listed the nations like a roll call of reasons: Amalekites in the Negev, Hittites, Jebusites, and Amorites in the hill country, Canaanites by the sea and along the Jordan. Caleb quieted the people before Moses and made the counter-case in one breath.
"We must go up and take possession of the land, for we can certainly conquer it!"
But the men who had gone up with him answered the opposite, and then the report changed character. It stopped being a survey and became a warning about the land itself.
"We cannot go up against the people, for they are stronger than we are!"
They gave the Israelites a bad report about the land they had spied out. The land devours its inhabitants, they said, and all the people we saw there are of great size.

"We even saw the Nephilim there," they said, giants they called "the descendants of Anak that come from the Nephilim!" And then the sentence the report is remembered by: "We seemed like grasshoppers in our own sight, and we must have seemed the same to them!"

Grasshoppers in our own sight. The sentence admits what the whole report was built on: the ten had measured the land by how small it made them feel, and brought the feeling back as if it were a fact about Canaan. The cluster of grapes on the pole said the land was good. The grasshopper sentence said the spies had already surrendered in it.
That night, the whole congregation lifted up their voices and cried out, and the people wept. All the Israelites grumbled against Moses and Aaron.

"If only we had died in the land of Egypt, or if only we had died in this wilderness! Why is the LORD bringing us into this land to fall by the sword? Our wives and children will become plunder. Would it not be better for us to go back to Egypt?"
And then the grumbling found its program, the most practical sentence of rebellion in the book.
"Let us appoint a leader and return to Egypt."

Moses and Aaron fell facedown before the whole assembly. Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh, who were among those who had spied out the land, tore their clothes and made the last appeal anyone would make to this generation.
"The land we passed through and explored is an exceedingly good land. If the LORD delights in us, He will bring us into this land, a land flowing with milk and honey, and He will give it to us."

"Only do not rebel against the LORD, and do not be afraid of the people of the land, for they will be like bread for us. Their protection has been removed, and the LORD is with us. Do not be afraid of them!"

The congregation's answer was to talk of stoning Joshua and Caleb. At that moment the glory of the LORD appeared to all the Israelites at the Tent of Meeting, and God spoke of ending the story altogether. How long will this people treat Me with contempt? How long will they refuse to believe in Me, despite all the signs I have performed among them? I will strike them with a plague and destroy them, and make you into a nation greater and mightier than they.

It was the golden calf offer again, nearly word for word: let Me start over with you, Moses. And Moses gave the same answer, expanded. The Egyptians will hear of it, and tell the Canaanites, who have already heard that God is among this people, seen face to face, His cloud standing over them, going before them in a pillar by day and fire by night. If You kill this people as one man, the nations will say the LORD was not able to bring them into the land He swore to give them, so He slaughtered them in the wilderness. Then Moses quoted God's own words from the mountain back to Him, the name God had proclaimed when Moses' face was still hidden in the rock.

"The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion, forgiving iniquity and transgression. Yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished; He will visit the iniquity of the fathers upon their children to the third and fourth generation."
"Pardon, I pray, the iniquity of this people, in keeping with the greatness of Your loving devotion, just as You have forgiven them ever since they left Egypt."
"I have pardoned them as you requested," the LORD replied.

And in the next sentence the pardon and the sentence arrive together, which is the shape of this whole book. As surely as I live, and as surely as the whole earth is filled with the glory of the LORD, none of the men who have seen My glory and the signs I performed in Egypt and in the wilderness, and who have tested Me these ten times and not obeyed Me, will ever see the land.
"Your bodies will fall in this wilderness"
All who were numbered in the census, everyone twenty years of age or older, would fall there, because they had grumbled against Him.
"Surely none of you will enter the land in which I swore to settle you, except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun."

Their children, the little ones the congregation had said would become plunder, those children God would bring in, and they would know the land their fathers rejected. As for the fathers: in keeping with the forty days they had spied out the land, they would bear their guilt forty years, a year for each day, wandering until the last of the counted generation had fallen. The ten spies who brought the bad report were struck down by a plague before the LORD, there in front of the camp they had panicked. Of the twelve who carried the grapes, only Joshua and Caleb remained alive.
Moses told the people these words, and they mourned bitterly. And early the next morning they got up and went up toward the ridge of the hill country, confessing as they climbed.
"We have indeed sinned," they said, "but we will go to the place the LORD has promised."

It was obedience, one day late, aimed at a door God had already closed. Moses warned them not to go, because the LORD was not among them, and they would be struck down. They went anyway, daring to climb, while neither Moses nor the ark of the covenant moved from the camp. The Amalekites and Canaanites who lived in that hill country came down, attacked them, and routed them all the way to Hormah. The generation that would not enter the land when God was with them tried to enter it when He was not, and got the war the ten spies had feared, without the God who would have won it.

Chapter 15 reads quietly after that, and its quiet is the point. God gave laws for offerings in the land the people would enter, grain and drink offerings measured against the animal, the same proportions for the burnt offering, the peace offering, and the sin offering for an unintentional sin, with one law for the native born and for the foreigner who lived among them. He gave the law of the first of the dough, offered as a contribution. He gave the warning that the person who sins defiantly, native or foreigner, blasphemes the LORD and is to be cut off, because he has despised the word of the LORD. These are instructions for a future the speakers would not live in, given to a camp under a sentence of death by wandering. God went on legislating for the land anyway. The promise had been delayed for the fathers. It had not been withdrawn from the children.

The chapter's one story is small and terrible. While the Israelites were in the wilderness, a man was found gathering wood on the Sabbath day. The men who found him brought him to Moses and Aaron and the whole congregation, and they placed him in custody, because it had not been made clear what should be done to him. The word came back.
"The man must surely be put to death. The whole congregation is to stone him outside the camp."

So the whole congregation took him outside the camp and stoned him to death, as the LORD had commanded Moses. In a book about a generation dying slowly, one man died quickly, for kindling, on the day of rest, before the wandering had properly begun.
And the chapter closes with a piece of clothing. God told Moses to have the Israelites make tassels for the corners of their garments throughout their generations, with a blue cord on each tassel.

"These will serve as tassels for you to look at, so that you may remember all the commandments of the LORD, that you may obey them and not prostitute yourselves by following your own heart and your own eyes."
"I am the LORD your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God. I am the LORD your God."

The verdict of the spies had come from following their own eyes: grasshoppers, in their own sight. The tassels were the counterweight, tied where a man could see them every day of the forty years, a reminder sewn onto the sentence itself.
The camp turned away from the border. It had thirty-eight years of wilderness in front of it, and almost none of what happened in them would be written down.

title: Korah and the Staff That Blossomed
subtitle: Numbers 16 to 19, Berean Standard Bible
description: Korah's rebellion is swallowed by the ground, Aaron stands between the living and the dead, and a dead staff blossoms.
paragraphs: The sentence had been handed down. The counted generation would die in the wilderness, and the camp had settled into the first stretch of those forty years. The next rebellion did not come from the edges of the camp, the way the complaints about food had. It came from the center, from the family that carried the ark.

Korah was a Levite, a son of Kohath: one of the men whose family bore the most holy things on their shoulders, covered, forbidden to touch them or look at them and live. With him came some Reubenites, Dathan and Abiram, sons of Eliab, and On son of Peleth, and behind all of them stood two hundred and fifty leaders of the congregation, men of renown, chosen from the assembly. The Reubenites' tents stood on the south side of the tabernacle, next to the Kohathites. The rebellion had an address, and the address was as close to the tent as a layman's tent could be.
They came together against Moses and Aaron with a charge built out of a truth.
"You have taken too much upon yourselves! For everyone in the entire congregation is holy, and the LORD is in their midst. Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?"

Everyone in the congregation was holy. God had said so Himself, in almost those words, back at the mountain. The claim was the claim Miriam and Aaron had made in smaller form, now with 250 leaders behind it: if God speaks to all, why do two brothers stand between Him and everyone else? Moses, who had once begged God not to make him a nation in Israel's place, heard the charge that he had made himself a king.

When Moses heard this, he fell facedown. Then he answered with a test instead of a defense. Tomorrow morning the LORD would reveal who belongs to Him and who is holy, and He would bring that person near to Himself. Korah and his company were to take censers, put fire and incense in them, and come before the LORD. The man God chose would be the holy one. Moses added the point the whole rebellion had stepped around: a censer is a priest's instrument. The Levites were about to try to do at the tent's entrance what Nadab and Abihu had died doing inside it.

Moses sent for Dathan and Abiram, and they refused the summons with a speech that showed how far the memory of Egypt had rotted. Is it not enough that you have brought us up out of a land flowing with milk and honey to kill us in the wilderness, that you also make yourself ruler over us? Egypt, called a land flowing with milk and honey: the phrase God used for Canaan, handed to the slave pits. And you have not brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey, they said, or given us an inheritance of fields and vineyards. Will you gouge out the eyes of these men? We will not come.

Moses was greatly angered, and he said to the LORD: do not accept their offering. I have not taken one donkey from them, and I have not wronged a single one of them. Then he spoke to Korah again, and this time his question went to the root of the man's own story. Moses reminded the sons of Levi what they already had: separated from the congregation of Israel, brought near to God to do the work of the tabernacle and stand before the congregation to minister to them, Korah and all his fellow Levites with him. Was that a small thing? He and his company were seeking the priesthood too.
"Therefore, it is you and all your followers who have conspired against the LORD! As for Aaron, who is he that you should grumble against him?"

The next morning Korah gathered his whole assembly against Moses and Aaron at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, and every man of the 250 stood with his censer and his fire. The glory of the LORD appeared to the whole congregation, and God spoke the sentence Moses had heard at the calf and at the spies: separate yourselves from this congregation, so that I may consume them in an instant.

Moses and Aaron fell facedown, and their intercession this time had a lawyer's precision. O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, will You be angry with the whole congregation when only one man has sinned? God narrowed the judgment to the households involved. The congregation was to move away from the dwellings of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram.

Moses went to the Reubenites' tents with the elders of Israel following him, and he warned the congregation to move back, and to touch nothing that belonged to these men, or be swept away in all their sins. The people moved back. Dathan and Abiram came out and stood at the entrances of their tents, with their wives, their sons, and their little children, a whole household lined up behind its father's rebellion. Korah stood with them there. Then Moses announced how the camp would know whose claim was true. If these men die a natural death, the LORD has not sent me.

"But if the LORD brings about something unprecedented, and the earth opens its mouth and swallows them and all that belongs to them so that they go down alive into Sheol, then you will know that these men have treated the LORD with contempt."

As soon as Moses finished saying all this, the ground beneath them split open. The earth opened its mouth and swallowed their households, Korah and all his men, and everything they owned. They went down alive into Sheol with all they owned, and the earth closed over them, and they vanished from the assembly. All Israel around them fled at their cries, shouting that the earth might swallow them too. And fire came forth from the LORD and consumed the 250 men who were offering the incense.

On son of Peleth, the fourth name in the rebellion's first verse, is never mentioned again in the chapter. The text does not say whether he went home before the morning, or what became of him. He simply disappears from the story between the conspiracy and the ground opening, and the record leaves him there.

The censers of the dead men were not thrown away. Eleazar son of Aaron gathered the bronze censers from the fire, the censers of men who had sinned at the cost of their lives, and had them hammered out as plating for the altar: a covering on the altar itself, a memorial to the Israelites that no outsider who is not a descendant of Aaron should come near to burn incense before the LORD, or he would become like Korah and his company. The altar the priests served at every morning now wore the flattened censers of the men who had tried to take the priesthood by claim. Every sacrifice after that was offered on top of the warning.
The next day, the whole congregation grumbled against Moses and Aaron with a sentence that shows how little the ground opening had settled.
"You have killed the LORD's people!"

God's anger answered it with a plague, and the plague moved faster than the argument. Get away from this congregation so that I may consume them in an instant, God said, and Moses and Aaron fell facedown. But this time Moses did not stay down. He told Aaron to take his censer, put fire from the altar and incense in it, and carry it quickly into the congregation to make atonement for them, because wrath had gone out from the LORD and the plague had begun. Aaron ran. He stood in among the dying with smoke rising from a priest's censer, the very instrument the 250 had died holding wrongly, and the text gives the picture in one line.
"He stood between the living and the dead, and the plague was halted."

The dead from the plague numbered 14,700, besides those who had died on account of Korah. Aaron walked back to Moses at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. The priesthood Korah had called a brother's power grab had just saved the congregation that was accusing it, with the high priest's own body as the wall.

One more sign was given, quieter than the earth and the fire, because the grumbling needed an answer that could be kept. Each leader of the twelve tribes was to bring a staff, his name written on it, Aaron's name on the staff of Levi. The staffs were laid up in the Tent of the Testimony before the LORD. The staff belonging to the man God chose would sprout.
"The next day Moses entered the Tent of the Testimony and saw that Aaron's staff, representing the house of Levi, had sprouted, put forth buds, blossomed, and produced almonds."

A dead stick, cut from a tree and carved into a walking staff, had run the whole course of a living branch in one night: buds, blossoms, and ripe almonds on the same wood. Moses brought all the staffs out and the Israelites looked at them, and each man took his own back, eleven pieces of dead wood and one that had flowered. The LORD told Moses to put Aaron's staff back in front of the Testimony, kept as a sign for the rebellious, to put an end to their grumbling. Israel's answer, when they saw it, was fear rather than peace: we are perishing, we are all perishing, everyone who comes near the tabernacle will die. Are we all to die?

Chapters 18 and 19 answer that fear with the structure Leviticus had built and Numbers now explained from the inside. Aaron and his sons bore responsibility for the sanctuary and the priesthood, a service given to them as a gift, with the warning that any outsider who came near would be put to death. The priests would have no inheritance of land among Israel.
"You will have no inheritance in their land, nor will you have any portion among them. I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites."

Their living came from the altar: the holy offerings, the wave offerings, the firstfruits and the firstborn given to them as an everlasting covenant of salt. The Levites received Israel's tithe, a tenth of everything, as their inheritance in return for their work at the tent, and from that tenth the Levites themselves gave a tenth of the best to the priests. The men Episode 1 had counted as a ring around the tent now had their whole economy explained: no fields, no vineyards, and a share of everything the other tribes grew and raised.

And for a camp that was going to spend forty years burying its own generation, chapter 19 gave the rite for death's uncleanness itself. A red heifer, unblemished, without defect, that had never been placed under a yoke, was given to Eleazar outside the camp, slaughtered in his presence, its blood sprinkled seven times toward the front of the Tent of Meeting. The whole animal was burned with cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet wool thrown into the fire. A man who was clean gathered the ashes and stored them in a clean place outside the camp, kept by the congregation for the water of purification. Mixed with fresh water, the ashes of one burned heifer cleansed the man who had touched a corpse, a bone, or a grave, sprinkled on the third day and the seventh, after which he washed and was clean at evening. The one who refused the water was cut off, because he had defiled the sanctuary of the LORD.

It was provision for the book's long middle. The camp that had just buried 14,700 of its own in a day was going to live among graves for decades, and every burial made someone unclean. God's answer was not to move the camp away from death. It was to keep a jar of ashes outside the camp, ready, so that death never had the last word on whether a man could come back in.

title: Water, a Serpent, and the End of the Old Road
subtitle: Numbers 20 and 21, Berean Standard Bible
description: Miriam and Aaron die, Moses strikes the rock, and the new generation wins its first land east of the Jordan.
paragraphs: Something is missing at the start of chapter 20, and the missing thing is about thirty-eight years.

The last episode closed with the camp digesting Korah's rebellion, still in the second year out of Egypt. This chapter opens in the first month, the whole congregation entering the wilderness of Zin and staying at Kadesh, and the first thing the text records is a burial.
"In the first month, the whole congregation of Israel entered the Wilderness of Zin and stayed in Kadesh. There Miriam died and was buried."

No year is named. The forty years of the sentence had nearly run. Miriam the prophetess, who had watched a baby in a basket on the Nile and led Israel's women in song on the far side of the sea, died at Kadesh with the land in sight, and the text gives her death one sentence and a grave. Between chapters 19 and 20 almost an entire generation had died the same way, unrecorded, one grave at a time in a wilderness that was never meant to hold them. The silence of those years is the loudest fact in the book of Numbers. It means the camp reading these chapters now was mostly a new people: the children of the spies chapter, grown, with their parents' graves behind them all the way back to Egypt.
And the first thing the new generation did at Kadesh was the old generation's act, word for word.

There was no water for the congregation, so they gathered against Moses and Aaron and quarreled with him. If only we had perished with our brothers before the LORD. Why have you brought the LORD's assembly into this wilderness for us and our livestock to die here? Why have you led us up out of Egypt to bring us to this wretched place?
"It is not a place of grain, figs, vines, or pomegranates" they said, "and there is no water to drink!"

Read that list against the book so far. Grain, figs, vines, pomegranates: it is the fruit of Canaan, the grapes of Eshcol and the spies' other samples, named by a generation that had grown up on manna within sight of the land that grew them. The complaint was inherited, but the thirst was real, and so was the place. Kadesh was where the spies had set out from. Israel was back at the scene of the sentence, nearly forty years later, making the same speech.

Moses and Aaron went to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting and fell facedown, and the glory of the LORD appeared to them. The instruction God gave was specific, and its details matter, because what Moses did next is measured against them.

"Take the staff and assemble the congregation. You and your brother Aaron are to speak to the rock while they watch, and it will pour out its water. You will bring out water from the rock and provide drink for the congregation and their livestock."

Moses took the staff from before the LORD, as commanded. Whether it was his own staff or Aaron's budding staff, kept in front of the Testimony as a sign, the text does not say, and the story does not depend on it. He and Aaron gathered the assembly in front of the rock. And then Moses spoke, not to the rock, but to the people.
"Listen now, you rebels, must we bring you water out of this rock?"

Then Moses raised his hand and struck the rock twice with his staff, and a great amount of water gushed out, and the congregation and their livestock drank. The miracle worked. God gave the water anyway, to the rebels and to the man who had disobeyed in front of them. And then God spoke to Moses and Aaron together.
"Because you did not trust Me to show My holiness in the sight of the Israelites, you will not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them."

These were the waters of Meribah, quarreling, where the Israelites quarreled with the LORD and He showed His holiness among them. The sentence that had fallen on a whole generation at the spies fell at the end of the wandering on the two men who had interceded for that generation at every step. Moses would see the land. He would not enter it. Aaron would not either. The text does not give Moses a speech of protest, or record Aaron saying anything at all. It moves on, the way the march moved on, and the next event is Israel asking Edom for the road.

Moses sent messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom with a message built on family: thus says your brother Israel. It rehearsed the whole story, the hardship in Egypt, the cry God heard, the angel, the Exodus, and asked only to pass through on the king's highway, not turning into field or vineyard, not drinking well water, until they had passed through his territory. Edom refused, with a sword behind the refusal: you may not pass through, or I will come out with the sword against you. Israel offered to pay for any water they or their livestock drank, and to come up by the highway only. Edom came out against them with a large and powerful army, and Israel turned away. The descendants of Esau barred the road to the descendants of Jacob, and Israel, who would within the year take land from kings who fought them, would not force a brother's border.

From Kadesh the whole congregation journeyed to Mount Hor, on the border of Edom, and there the second of the three burials of Exodus' leadership was carried out in public, almost like a ceremony, because it was one. God told Moses that Aaron would be gathered to his people and would not enter the land, because both of them had rebelled against His command at the waters of Meribah. Aaron was to be taken up Mount Hor in the sight of the whole congregation, with Eleazar his son.
"So Moses did as the LORD had commanded, and they climbed Mount Hor in the sight of the whole congregation."
"After Moses had removed Aaron's garments and put them on his son Eleazar, Aaron died there on top of the mountain. Then Moses and Eleazar came down from the mountain."

The high priest's robes, the blue and purple and scarlet, the breastpiece with the stones, the gold plate on the turban, were taken off the old man on the mountaintop and put on his son in front of the watching nation below, and the new high priest walked back down the mountain wearing them, next to Moses, alone. When the whole congregation saw that Aaron had died, all the house of Israel mourned for him thirty days. Aaron was 123 years old when he died on Mount Hor. He had spoken for his brother before Pharaoh, built the calf, worn the garments, carried the censer between the living and the dead, and outlived two of his own sons. He died within sight of the land's border, in the office he handed over standing up.

Chapter 21 opens with Israel attacked for the first time by a king who came to them. The Canaanite king of Arad, in the Negev, heard that Israel was coming and attacked them and captured some prisoners. Israel vowed a vow: if God would deliver this people into their hands, they would devote their cities to destruction. God heard, and delivered up the Canaanites, and the place was named Hormah, destruction: the same Hormah where the counted generation had been routed when it tried to enter the land without God. The children won their first battle on the ground of their fathers' defeat.

Then the road bent away from the border again, around Edom, and patience broke for the last recorded time in the old style. The people grew impatient on the journey and spoke against God and against Moses.
"Why have you led us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? There is no bread or water, and we detest this wretched food!"

God sent venomous snakes among the people, and many Israelites were bitten and died. This time the people came to Moses with the confession ready: we have sinned, for we have spoken against the LORD and against you. Intercede with the LORD to take the snakes away from us. Moses prayed for the people, the same Moses, the same prayer, forty years in. God's remedy was strange and specific, and it was not to take the snakes away.
"Make a fiery serpent and mount it on a pole. When anyone who is bitten looks at it, he will live."
"So Moses made a bronze snake and mounted it on a pole. If anyone who was bitten looked at the bronze snake, he would live."

The camp was full of dying people looking up at a bronze copy of the thing that was killing them, lifted where everyone could see it, and living. The snakes stayed. The dying had a place to look. Centuries later, Israel's own kings would have to destroy that same bronze serpent, because the people had started burning incense to it, but that is Kings' story, not Numbers'. Here it is what God made it: the means of life, raised on a pole in a camp of bitten people.

From Mount Hor the journey turned, station by station, and the text starts singing. At Beer, the well, Israel sang a song to the water: spring up, O well, sing to it, the well the princes dug. A book in the narrative called the Book of the Wars of the LORD is quoted for a line about the Arnon, the river that marks Moab's border, because Israel was now moving through country with borders and kings, and the road was finally going somewhere.

Sihon king of the Amorites, who ruled in Heshbon, got the same message Edom had gotten: let us pass through your land, on the king's highway, turning aside into no field or vineyard. Edom had refused and Israel had turned away. Sihon refused differently. He gathered his whole army and went out to confront Israel in the wilderness, and fought them at Jahaz.
"And Israel put him to the sword and took possession of his land, from the Arnon to the Jabbok"
The advance stopped only at the border of the Ammonites, because that border was fortified.

It was not a skirmish. Israel took all his cities and settled in them, Heshbon and all its surrounding villages, land that Sihon himself had taken from a former king of Moab, as the proverb makers quoted in the text recalled. Moses sent spies to Jazer and Israel took its towns. Then the road turned up toward Bashan, and Og came out.

Og king of Bashan came out against them at Edrei, he and all his people, the second king in a row to march out and meet Israel in open battle. God's word to Moses before this fight was the word the spies' generation had died refusing to believe.
"Do not fear him, for I have delivered him into your hand, along with all his people and his land. Do to him as you did to Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon."
"So they struck down Og, along with his sons and his whole army, until no remnant was left. And they took possession of his land."

Two kings, two armies, and a stretch of country east of the Jordan, all before Israel had crossed the river. The generation that had seemed like grasshoppers in its own sight had died in the wilderness, down to nearly the last man. Its children had just taken the land of giants without a speech about grasshoppers anywhere in the chapter.
Then the Israelites traveled on and camped in the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho. From that camp, a king who had watched all of this happen went looking for a prophet to hire.

title: Balaam and the Fall at Peor
subtitle: Numbers 22 to 25, Berean Standard Bible
description: Balak hires Balaam to curse Israel and gets blessings instead, but at Peor the camp wounds itself.
paragraphs: Moab watched Israel take the land of two kings, and Moab was afraid. The Moabites said to the elders of Midian that this horde would devour everything around them, as an ox licks up the grass of the field. Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, did not march out the way Sihon and Og had marched out. He went shopping for a weapon armies could not answer: a curse, professionally delivered.
His messengers went to Pethor, by the Euphrates, to Balaam son of Beor, a man with an international reputation in exactly that trade.

"Behold, a people has come out of Egypt," said Balak. "They cover the face of the land and have settled next to me. So please come now and put a curse on this people, because they are too mighty for me. Perhaps I may be able to defeat them and drive them out of the land; for I know that those you bless are blessed, and those you curse are cursed."

The elders of Moab and Midian came to Balaam with the fees for divination in their hands, and Balaam did the professionally correct thing: stay the night, and I will bring back word, as the LORD may speak to me. God came to Balaam that night and asked who the men were, and gave His answer before the negotiation could start.
"Do not go with them. You are not to curse this people, for they are blessed."

Balaam sent the princes home with a polite refusal: the LORD has refused to let me go with you. Balak, who understood the market, sent a second delegation, more princes and more distinguished than the first, carrying a bigger offer. I will honor you richly and do whatever you say. Balaam's answer to the servants is the answer of a man saying the right thing and hoping the circumstances change.
Balaam's reply is on the record: "If Balak were to give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not do anything small or great to go beyond the command of the LORD my God."

Then he added the sentence that undid it: stay here tonight as well, and I will find out what else the LORD will speak to me. God came that night and permitted the trip, with a leash on it. Since these men have come to summon you, get up and go with them, but you must only do what I tell you. Balaam saddled his donkey in the morning and went. And God's anger was kindled because he went, a sentence the text states flatly after stating the permission flatly, and leaves standing there, unexplained, the way this book leaves its hardest sentences. The road itself delivered the commentary.

The donkey saw what the seer could not. The angel of the LORD was standing in the road with a drawn sword in his hand, and the donkey turned off the path into a field, and Balaam beat her to return her to the path. The angel stood in a narrow lane between vineyards, wall on this side and wall on that, and the donkey pressed against the wall and crushed Balaam's foot against it, and he beat her again. The angel moved ahead to a narrow place where there was no way to turn right or left, and the donkey lay down under Balaam, and Balaam's anger burned and he beat her with his staff.
Then the LORD opened the donkey's mouth, and she said to Balaam: "What have I done to you that you have beaten me these three times?"

Balaam answered the animal, mid-argument, before the strangeness of it seems to have reached him: because you have made a fool of me. If I had a sword in my hand, I would kill you right now. He was standing in a road telling his donkey he wished he had a sword, while a drawn sword he could not see was the whole reason for the conversation.
But the donkey said to Balaam: "Am I not the donkey you have ridden all your life until today? Have I ever treated you this way before?" He replied: "No."

Then the LORD opened Balaam's eyes, and he saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road with the sword drawn, and Balaam bowed low and fell facedown. The angel asked him the donkey's question in heaven's wording: why have you beaten your donkey these three times? I have come out to oppose you, because your way is perverse before me. The donkey saw me and turned away these three times. If she had not turned away, I would surely have killed you by now, and spared her.
"I have sinned," Balaam said to the angel of the LORD, "for I did not realize that you were standing in the road to confront me. And now, if this is displeasing in your sight, I will go back home."

The offer to go back was allowed to pass. Go with the men, the angel said, but you are to speak only what I tell you. The prophet who charged kings for curses arrived in Moab with his fee on the table and his mouth under orders, and he told Balak the terms to his face.
"See, I have come to you," Balaam replied, "but can I say just anything? I must speak only the word that God puts in my mouth."

Balak built the curse like a siege. At Bamoth-baal, from which Balaam could see the outskirts of the camp, Balak sacrificed oxen and sheep, and Balaam had him build seven altars and prepare seven bulls and seven rams. Balaam went off alone to a barren height to meet God, and God met him, and put a word in his mouth. He came back and stood beside the burnt offering, with all the princes of Moab standing there waiting for a curse, and he opened his mouth and delivered the first oracle. Balak brought me from Aram to curse Jacob and denounce Israel, it began. How can I curse what God has not cursed? From the top of the rocks I see him, a people dwelling alone, not counting itself among the nations.
"Who can count the dust of Jacob or number even a fourth of Israel? Let me die the death of the righteous; let my end be like theirs!"

Balak's response was commercial, not theological: what have you done to me? I brought you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have only blessed them. Balaam reminded him of the leash. Balak, like any buyer, changed the location and ordered another attempt: come to another place, where you will see the edge of them but not all of them, and curse them for me from there. Seven more altars on the top of Pisgah, seven more bulls, seven more rams. God met Balaam again. The second oracle is the one preachers have quoted ever since, and it landed in a hired curse-session on a mountaintop in Moab.
"God is not a man, that He should lie, or a son of man, that He should change His mind. Does He speak and not act? Does He promise and not fulfill?"
"I have indeed received a command to bless; He has blessed, and I cannot change it."

He sees no trouble for Israel, the oracle went on. The LORD their God is with them, and the shout of the King is among them. God brought them out of Egypt with the strength of the wild ox. There is no spell against Jacob and no divination against Israel. Balak tried a third arrangement, and this time his instructions show a man managing a defective product: do not curse them at all, and do not bless them at all, either. Balaam answered that he had told the messengers from the beginning that he could only speak what the LORD said. Balak took him up anyway, to the top of Peor, overlooking the wilderness. Seven altars again. Twenty-one bulls and twenty-one rams had now been burned across three mountaintops to purchase one sentence against Israel, and the sentence would not come.

At Peor, Balaam stopped waiting for a chance encounter. He saw that it pleased the LORD to bless Israel, and he did not go as at other times to seek omens, but set his face toward the wilderness. He lifted up his eyes and saw Israel camping tribe by tribe, the square of standards from Episode 1 laid out below him, and the Spirit of God came upon him. The third oracle opens on the camp itself.
"How lovely are your tents, O Jacob, your dwellings, O Israel!"

Like valleys stretching out, like gardens beside a river, like aloes the LORD has planted. Water will flow from their buckets and their seed will have abundant water. Their king will be greater than Agag, and their kingdom exalted. And it closed with a line Balak had paid a fortune trying to reverse.

The oracle pictured Israel crouching and lying down "like a lion, like a lioness" that no one dares to rouse, and it ended where it had to end for Balak: "Blessed are those who bless you and cursed are those who curse you."

Balak's anger burned against Balaam, and he struck his hands together. I summoned you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have persisted in blessing them these three times. Now flee to your homeland. I said I would honor you richly, but the LORD has held you back from honor. Balaam reminded him, one more time, of the fine print he had announced to every messenger: even if Balak gave him his house full of silver and gold, he could not go beyond the command of the LORD. And before he left, he gave Balak, unasked, one final oracle, about what this people would do to Moab in the latter days. Out of it comes the book's most far-reaching sentence, spoken by a hired prophet on his way home unpaid.
"I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near. A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel. He will crush the skulls of Moab and strike down all the sons of Sheth."

Oracles followed over Edom, Amalek, the Kenites, Asshur, and Eber, and then Balaam rose and went back to his place, and Balak also went his way. The curse had failed completely. No spell, no divination, no mountain, no fee had moved God's word one inch. Israel, camped in its square below, had not heard a syllable of any of it. The whole war had been fought over their heads, on three mountains, and they had won it without knowing it was happening.
What they could not survive was their own camp, at a place called Shittim.

While Israel was staying in Shittim, the men began to indulge in sexual immorality with the daughters of Moab. The women invited the people to the sacrifices of their gods, and the people ate and bowed down to their gods.
"So Israel joined in worshiping Baal of Peor, and the anger of the LORD burned against them."

The LORD told Moses to take all the leaders of the people and execute them in broad daylight before the LORD, so that His fierce anger would turn away from Israel, and Moses told Israel's judges to each kill his own men who had joined in worshiping Baal of Peor. A plague was already moving through the camp. And while the whole congregation was weeping at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, an Israelite man walked in front of Moses and everyone, bringing a Midianite woman into camp, to his family. The text names him when the act is done: Zimri son of Salu, a leader of a Simeonite family. The woman was Cozbi, daughter of Zur, a leader of a Midianite clan. A prince of Simeon and a princess of Midian, in the middle of a plague, in front of the weeping congregation, a deliberate display.

The text records that Phinehas son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, got up from the assembly and took a spear in his hand. He followed the Israelite into the tent and drove the spear through both of them, through the Israelite and on through the belly of the woman. "So the plague against the Israelites was halted."

The dead from the plague numbered 24,000. Phinehas was Aaron's grandson, Eleazar's son, the third generation of the priesthood Leviticus had ordained, and God's word on his act was not a rebuke for violence but a covenant.
"Phinehas son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, has turned My wrath away from the Israelites; for he was zealous for My sake among them, so that I did not consume the Israelites in My zeal."

"Declare, therefore, that I am granting him My covenant of peace. It will be a covenant of permanent priesthood for him and his descendants, because he was zealous for his God and made atonement for the Israelites."

And the book's last word on the whole Moab affair is a command that reaches forward into Episode 8's generation: attack the Midianites and strike them dead, because they assailed Israel deceitfully when they seduced them in the matter of Peor, and in the matter of Cozbi, their sister, the woman killed on the day the plague came because of Peor.

Set the two halves of this episode side by side, because the book sets them that way. On the mountains, a pagan king spent twenty-one bulls, twenty-one rams, and a promised fortune, and could not buy one curse against Israel. In the valley, Israel cursed itself for the price of a dinner invitation and a god's feast, and 24,000 died. The camp Balaam had blessed from above, tribe by tribe in its perfect square, was counted again in the next chapter, because after Peor a new census was not paperwork anymore.
It was a roll call of who was left.

title: A New Generation Counted
subtitle: Numbers 26 to 36, Berean Standard Bible
description: A new generation is counted, five daughters change the inheritance law, Joshua is commissioned, and the book ends facing the river.
paragraphs: God told Moses and Eleazar to count Israel again.

The Aaron in that sentence is gone.
